scenario.prompt_to_agent:
Helpdesk ticket #8877: Since a firewall change window this morning, BOTH pods
have lost access to every 10.200.0.x server: DNS queries to 10.200.0.2 time
out and no portal loads by name or by IP. Pod-to-pod traffic between
host_1_1_1_1 and host_2_1_1_1 still works. Monitoring shows all OSPF
adjacencies Full and the 10.200.0.0/24 route present on every router.
Identify what is blocking the server farm.

injection.action: add a FORWARD DROP rule for all traffic destined to the server farm

scenario.ground_truth:
Affected component: router_core_3 iptables FORWARD chain
Mechanism: router_core_3 is the mandatory transit for the server farm --
  switch_server_access attaches only to router_core_3 (172.16.0.10/31). The
  new rule `-A FORWARD -d 10.200.0.0/24 -j DROP` silently discards every
  FORWARDED packet destined to the farm, from both pods. Routing is
  genuinely healthy: OSPF hellos are INPUT/OUTPUT traffic on router_core_3
  (not FORWARD), so all adjacencies stay Full and 10.200.0.0/24 remains in
  every table -- the drop happens at the firewall layer after the routing
  decision. Pod-to-pod traffic transits router_core_1<->router_core_2 and
  matches no rule. Note: router_core_3's OWN pings to the farm still succeed
  (locally generated traffic traverses OUTPUT, not FORWARD) -- a useful
  discriminator.
Localization: router_core_3
Root cause: extraneous iptables FORWARD DROP rule for destination
  10.200.0.0/24 on router_core_3
Fix: `iptables -D FORWARD -d 10.200.0.0/24 -j DROP` on router_core_3
scenario.fix_spec:
remove the DROP rule on router_core_3 --
`iptables -D FORWARD -d 10.200.0.0/24 -j DROP`
scoring_axes: must-identify-component: iptables FORWARD DROP rule / firewall filter, not a routing fault
must-recognize-filter-pattern: recognizes that healthy OSPF plus present routes with silent forwarding loss indicates packet filtering on the transit path
bonus-notes-transit-choke: notes all farm traffic must transit router_core_3 (sole attachment of switch_server_access), which is why both pods are affected

agent.diagnosis_text:
The affected component is the host-based firewall on router_core_3 (iptables). Traffic from both pods to the server farm (10.200.0.0/24) must traverse router_core_3: on router_core_1 the route to 10.200.0.0/24 points to 172.16.0.3 (core_3 eth0), and on router_core_2 it points to 172.16.0.5 (core_3 eth1). On router_core_3 we found an explicit FORWARD-chain drop: “-A FORWARD -d 10.200.0.0/24 -j DROP” with counters showing hits (44 packets/3696 bytes). This explains why pod-to-pod traffic is unaffected (not destined to 10.200.0.0/24), why router_core_3 itself can ping 10.200.0.2 (local OUTPUT chain, not FORWARD), and why switch_server_access and servers can talk among themselves (same L2 segment, no forwarding). It also matches the helpdesk timeline of a firewall change.

Localization: router_core_3 iptables, FORWARD chain, impacting transits arriving on eth0/eth1 (from cores 1/2) and exiting toward eth2 (to switch_server_access). Routing/OSPF is healthy and consistent on all routers; the block is purely a filter.

Root cause: a change window introduced an iptables rule on router_core_3 that drops all forwarded traffic destined to 10.200.0.0/24.

Corrective fix: remove or supersede the rule on router_core_3 (e.g., iptables -D FORWARD -d 10.200.0.0/24 -j DROP), or insert explicit ACCEPT rules for required flows before any drop. Ensure the corrected policy is saved to persist across reboots/change rollbacks.

per_axis.rationale: The agent explicitly localizes the fault to router_core_3 (router_core_3 iptables FORWARD chain).

per_axis.axis: must-identify-component: iptables FORWARD DROP rule / firewall filter, not a routing fault
per_axis.rationale: The report clearly identifies an iptables FORWARD-chain DROP on router_core_3 as the cause and rules out a routing fault.

per_axis.axis: must-recognize-filter-pattern: recognizes that healthy OSPF plus present routes with silent forwarding loss indicates packet filtering on the transit path
per_axis.rationale: Agent explicitly notes OSPF/routes are healthy yet forwarded packets to 10.200.0.0/24 are silently dropped and identifies an iptables FORWARD DROP on router_core_3 as the filter causing the transit packet loss.

per_axis.axis: bonus-notes-transit-choke: notes all farm traffic must transit router_core_3 (sole attachment of switch_server_access), which is why both pods are affected
per_axis.rationale: Explicitly states that all traffic to 10.200.0.0/24 must traverse router_core_3 (routes on core_1/core_2 point to core_3 and transits arrive on eth0/eth1 and exit toward the server-facing interface), explaining why both pods are affected.
Recommends removing the FORWARD DROP rule (or inserting ACCEPT before it) on router_core_3 and saving the policy, which matches the expected fix.

The log shows an explicit FORWARD-chain DROP for destination 10.200.0.0/24 on router_core_3 and a pattern of successful local/router_core_3-originated pings but failures from pods — the observations support the firewall being the cause. The agent checked other devices' iptables and used directional pings to distinguish OUTPUT vs FORWARD behavior, so the inference is well supported with minor unshown routing-table details.
